Hand someone a coffee mug and then ask what they would sell it for. Ask a second person, who has no mug, what they would pay for one. The two numbers should be close. They are not. The owner wants roughly twice what the buyer offers, and the gap does not shrink when the mug is replaced with a pen, a chocolate bar or a lottery ticket.

The usual name for this is loss aversion: a loss of a given size hurts more than a gain of the same size pleases. The claim is narrow and the evidence for it is wide, which is the combination worth writing about.

## The shape of the asymmetry

Three features recur across the experiments.

- The reference point moves. What counts as a loss depends on what you expected to have, not on what you have.
- The curve is steeper on the loss side. A small loss is felt more sharply than a small gain, and the difference persists as the stakes rise.
- Ownership itself shifts the reference point. Holding the mug for five minutes is enough.

> Losing a hundred dollars stings about twice as much as finding a hundred dollars pleases.

That ratio is repeated so often that it has become a slogan, which is a reason to read past it. It is an average over a particular kind of gamble, not a constant of nature, and it varies with the person, the stake and the framing.

## Why it matters for how we think

This essay is less interested in the mug than in what the mug reveals about judgement. A mind that weighs losses twice is not making an arithmetic error; it is applying a rule that served it well when a lost meal mattered more than a found one. The Garden's note on [[Cognitive Psychology]] sketches the broader field, and the habit of testing yourself before you look, described under [[Active Recall|active recall]], is one place the same asymmetry shows up in learning: the sting of a failed retrieval teaches more than the comfort of a reread.

What follows from this is modest. Expect the asymmetry in yourself, name the reference point before deciding, and treat any choice framed as avoiding a loss with the suspicion it deserves. None of that removes the bias. It only makes the bias visible, which is the most an essay can do.
